title: Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction, and Polarisation

questions.question: In Young's double-slit experiment, the slit separation is 0.4 mm, the screen is 1.6 m away, and light of wavelength 500 nm is used. What is the fringe width?
questions.rationale: Fringe width = lambdaD/d = (500 x 10^-9 x 1.6)/(0.4 x 10^-3) = 2 x 10^-3 m = 2 mm. Halving the slit separation would double it, but with the given numbers the answer is 2 mm.

questions.question: What is the path difference for destructive interference at a point on the screen?
questions.rationale: Crest meets trough when the path difference is (2n+1)lambda/2, i.e. odd multiples of half a wavelength. Whole multiples of lambda give constructive interference instead.

questions.question: The entire Young's double-slit apparatus is immersed in water. What happens to the fringe width?
options: Decreases, because the wavelength in water is shorter
Stays the same, since frequency is unchanged
questions.rationale: In water the wavelength becomes lambda/n, so beta = (lambda/n)D/d decreases by the factor n (about 4/3). Fringes crowd closer together under water.

questions.question: If one of the two slits in Young's experiment is covered, what is observed on the screen?
options: The interference fringes vanish; only a broad single-slit diffraction pattern remains
questions.rationale: Interference needs two coherent waves. With one slit open there is nothing to interfere with, so the screen shows only the single-slit diffraction envelope — a broad central maximum with weak side bands.

questions.question: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on a single slit of width 0.02 mm. At what angle is the first diffraction minimum formed?
questions.rationale: First minimum: a sin(theta) = lambda, so sin(theta) = 600x10^-9 / 0.02x10^-3 = 0.03, giving theta of about 1.7 degrees. Small angles keep the central maximum narrow for wide slits.

questions.question: Which phenomenon proves conclusively that light waves are transverse?
questions.rationale: Only transverse waves can have a vibration direction to filter, so only they can be polarised. Sound (longitudinal) shows interference and diffraction but never polarisation.

questions.question: Unpolarised light strikes a glass surface (n = 1.5) at Brewster's angle. What is the angle of refraction?
questions.rationale: Brewster's angle: tan(theta_p) = 1.5, so theta_p of incidence is about 57 degrees. At Brewster incidence the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so the angle of refraction is 90 - 57 = 33 degrees.

questions.question: Two polaroids have their axes at 60 degrees. If unpolarised light of intensity I0 falls on the first, what intensity emerges from the second?
questions.rationale: The first polaroid halves any unpolarised beam: I0/2. Malus's law then gives the second transmission as (I0/2)cos^2(60) = (I0/2)(1/4) = I0/8.

questions.question: Why do anti-reflection coatings on camera lenses look bluish-purple?
options: The coating absorbs red light completely
Destructive interference cancels reflection strongest around green-yellow, so the residual reflected light is richer in red and violet
The coating polarises the reflected light
Glass itself is purple at the surface
questions.rationale: The quarter-wave coating is tuned so reflections from its two surfaces destructively interfere near the middle of the visible spectrum (green-yellow). What little light still reflects is dominated by the spectral ends — red and violet — mixing into a bluish-purple tint.

questions.question: A telescope's main mirror is replaced by one of twice the diameter, observing at the same wavelength. The smallest resolvable angular separation:
questions.rationale: Rayleigh's criterion gives theta_min = 1.22 lambda/D. Doubling the aperture D halves theta_min, so the telescope resolves details twice as close together — resolution improves in direct proportion to aperture.
